Hi Hannah,

Thanks again for taking a look — we are kicking off an internal review for our Private deployment with Redwood and have a few overlapping questions around certificates and DNS for our internal domains (acme.internal and svc.acme.internal). Current constraints:
- We run two VPCs (prod/us-west-2, prod-eu), each with private hosted zones.
- On-prem footprint for a subset of services in a colo, reaching the same internal domain names.
- Security wants a clear plan for cert ownership, rotation cadence, and who holds the private keys (customer CA vs Redwood-managed).

Specific asks:
1) Do you recommend SAN per service (service1.svc.acme.internal) vs a single wildcard (*.svc.acme.internal) for internal TLS?
2) Best practice for split-horizon DNS across cloud and colo so we can point services to local LB without leaking names publicly.
3) How does Redwood recommend terminating TLS for private endpoints — edge proxy in the VPC with mTLS to backend, or pass-through and let services terminate?

I attached our current_network_diagram.pdf. Can we get a short proposal + recommended configuration to present to our security and infra panels next week?

Appreciate it,

Subject: Re: Private endpoints cert strategy + DNS for acme.internal

Alice — thanks for the clear list. High level summary up front: we typically recommend SAN-scoped certificates (one cert per service/FQDN) for private deployments unless you have a very large ephemeral fleet that benefits from wildcards. Below are pros/cons and a recommended configuration for Acme.

Quick take:
- SAN-per-FQDN (recommended):
  - Pros: explicit mapping between cert and service, simpler revocation and audit, better compatibility with mTLS client validation and per-service identity.
  - Cons: more certs to manage, requires automated rotation tooling (we provide rotation_playbook patterns).
- Wildcard (*.svc.acme.internal):
  - Pros: fewer certs, easier for many short-lived subdomains.
  - Cons: broader blast radius if compromised, harder to restrict client CN/OU for mTLS, tricky with multiple tenant zones.

DNS and split-horizon guidance:
- Use private hosted zones scoped per VPC and create a consolidation layer in the colo for on-prem resolution.
- Implement conditional forwarders from on-prem DNS to the VPC private hosted zone for service discovery.
- Avoid public DNS entries for acme.internal; put health-check and external facing hostnames in acme.com only.

TLS termination patterns we see customers adopt:
1) Edge-termination (recommended default for Redwood Private): internal edge proxy inside the VPC terminates client TLS (mTLS optional), performs routing and then mTLS to backend services where required. This gives centralized observability in Redwood Console and simpler cert distribution if the edge can access the CA/KMS.
2) End-to-end mTLS: terminate at both edge and service (double-terminate), particularly for highly regulated workloads. Requires per-service certs and automated sync.
3) Passthrough: edge SNI routing without termination; useful when customers insist on service-owned keys and HSM-isolated private keys. Operational complexity is higher.

Key operational notes:
- Key ownership: if Acme requires HSM-managed keys inside your KMS, we support integrating with customer KMS/HSM for cert issuance and signing. In that case, Redwood will reference keys but not export them.
- Rotation cadence: recommend 30-90 day rotations for internal certs if you use short TTLs and automated deployment; conservative customers choose 180 days.
- Auditing: enable detailed TLS traces in Redwood Console and forward audit logs to your SIEM (we include the forwarding integration in the Private spec).

I've attached a short primer and a rotation playbook that map to the options above. My suggested next steps:
- Option A (Default): SAN-per-FQDN, edge proxy terminates + mTLS to services, Redwood reads signing certs from your KMS (HSM) via our connector.
- Option B (Strict): Per-service certs stored in on-prem HSM, passthrough/LB + service termination with automation for rotation.

If you want, we can sketch an explicit DNS record map for your two VPCs and colo and a cert matrix for the services you listed.

Cheers,
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

+1 to Hannah's recommendation. A couple of operational details from infra perspective: 

- DNS TTL and propagation: use short TTLs (30-60s) on LB A records used for canary/rollouts; keep SRV/CNAMEs for service discovery. For split-horizon, ensure your on-prem forwarders use conditional forwarding to the VPC resolver endpoints to avoid stale records.
- K8s secret sync: if you run microservices in k8s, sync certs from the central vault into namespace secrets via a controller; avoid mounting raw private keys on nodes when using HSM-backed signing.
- Health checks: if edge is terminating TLS and probing backends, use a separate health endpoint authenticated by a short-lived client cert. This prevents health probes from being treated as regular traffic for mTLS policy checks.

On wildcard vs SAN: operationally, wildcards reduce churn but if you plan to do per-service RBAC or tracing (client cert pins), you will want service identities.

-Dev
Dev Patel
Deployment Infrastructure, Redwood Inference

Thanks team — adding a security lens: 

- Audit and proof of rotation: add a per-rotation artifact (signed statement including cert thumbprint, time, and triggering commit id) and ship to Acme's central audit bucket. Redwood can push rotation events to your SIEM.
- Pins and identity: if you go SAN-per-FQDN, use SAN to embed role claims (CN or subjectAltName with OID) so the backend can enforce role-based access without additional lookups.
- Mutual TLS: recommend mTLS on two planes for sensitive services — edge->gateway (tls termination with client validation) and gateway->service (identity token via mTLS). This also allows us to keep short-lived service certs and rotate more aggressively.

Action items I propose:
1) Hannah: produce a cert matrix (who owns keys, TTL, signing CA, rotation cadence) per service — include staging/prod differences.
2) Dev: provide an example k8s secret sync manifest and conditional forwarder config.
3) Acme: confirm whether keys must remain in your on-prem HSM or if you will permit Redwood to reference them via a connector.

I can join the design review with Acme security Monday if helpful.

- Grace O'Connor
